title: The Crash
kicker: A violent equity-market break abruptly changed the hierarchy of risks and accelerated a flight toward government bonds.
known: Long-term Treasury yields had been elevated before the crash, leaving duration already under pressure.
The market break forced investors to reassess growth, liquidity and the expected path of monetary policy.

title: The Great Bond Massacre
kicker: The Federal Reserve began tightening and duration risk moved from background concern to the center of the market.
known: Economic momentum was strengthening and the market was increasingly vulnerable to a faster policy normalization.
The first tightening move challenged portfolios positioned for a more benign rate path.

title: The Flight to Safety
kicker: Russia's default accelerated a global move toward liquidity and exposed the fragility of leveraged relative-value positions.
known: Emerging-market stress was already visible after the Asian financial crisis.
The default intensified the demand for liquid, high-quality assets and set the stage for the LTCM crisis.

title: The Dot-Com Peak
kicker: The equity boom reached its peak while long-term yields remained high and the late-cycle policy environment was still restrictive.
known: Technology valuations were extreme and monetary conditions were no longer as supportive as they had been earlier in the expansion.
The subsequent transition was gradual: weaker investment and earnings preceded the 2001 recession.

title: The System Breaks
kicker: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. Funding stress moved from a sector problem toward a systemic crisis.
known: Lehman Brothers had filed for bankruptcy and funding conditions were under severe pressure.
Credit spreads had already widened materially, while the Federal Reserve's target rate remained at 2 percent.
The scale of the recession, future emergency facilities and the eventual path of Treasury yields were not yet known.

title: The Sovereign Crisis
kicker: Sovereign stress intensified as investors questioned fiscal sustainability and the architecture of the euro area.
chartTitle: U.S. safe-haven rates during euro stress
known: Sovereign spreads across the euro area had widened sharply and the banking-sovereign feedback loop was increasingly visible.
Safe-haven demand continued to support U.S. Treasuries.

title: The Taper Tantrum
kicker: A change in expectations around Federal Reserve asset purchases was enough to reprice global duration.
chartTitle: Treasury repricing after the taper signal
known: The Federal Reserve had begun discussing the conditions under which asset purchases might eventually slow.
Long-end yields were starting to reflect less certainty around the persistence of extraordinary policy support.

title: The Curve Inverts
kicker: The Treasury market was challenging the late-cycle growth narrative and pricing a greater probability of future easing.
known: Global manufacturing had weakened and the Federal Reserve had already pivoted away from its prior tightening path.
The curve was signaling vulnerability, not the specific catalyst of the recession that eventually followed.

title: The Liquidity Shock
kicker: The pandemic shock drove Treasury yields to extraordinary lows before the global demand for cash began to overwhelm market intermediation.
known: Global growth expectations were collapsing and emergency policy easing had already begun.
The next phase would reveal that even the Treasury market could suffer dysfunction when the demand for cash became extreme.

title: The Great Repricing
kicker: Persistent inflation forced a 75-basis-point Federal Reserve hike and accelerated the reset in nominal and real rates.
chartTitle: Treasury yields through the inflation repricing
known: Inflation had proven broader and more persistent than expected, forcing markets to repeatedly revise the policy path higher.
The bond market was moving from a low-rate regime into a materially different cost-of-capital environment.
